name: Vertical
description: Widescreen HD turned on its side: the shape of a phone held upright, used for video made to be watched on phones.
The old 4:3 television shape turned on its side, used for some vertical video.

name: Movietone
description: The nearly square frame of early sound films (about 1926 to 1932), left over when an optical soundtrack was added beside the silent-era picture. Seen in Sunrise (1927) and M (1931), and revived for The Lighthouse (2019).
Slightly squarer than a classic TV picture: the shape of early 405-line television broadcasts, and later of many computer monitors.

name: Fullscreen
description: The shape of silent films and of television before HD. A modern widescreen TV shows it with black bars on the left and right.

name: Academy ratio
description: The Hollywood standard set by the Academy in 1932, used for nearly all films until widescreen took over in 1953. Almost identical to 4:3.

name: IMAX
description: The tall frame of IMAX 70 mm film, which only the largest IMAX theaters can show at its full height.
The shape of a 35 mm still photograph and of the VistaVision film frame. Uncommon for a finished film or show.
A compromise between 4:3 and 16:9, devised after BBC audience tests, that broadcasters used to show a picture acceptably on both old and widescreen TVs.
The shape of many widescreen computer monitors and laptops of the 2000s, before they moved to 16:9. Rare for a film or show.

name: European widescreen
description: An early widescreen shape introduced by Paramount, which became the standard for theatrical films in several European countries. Also the native shape of Super 16 film.

name: European widescreen
description: Usually written 1.66:1: an early widescreen shape introduced by Paramount, which became the standard for theatrical films in several European countries. Also the native shape of Super 16 film.
An early widescreen shape used by MGM and Warner Bros. from 1953 to 1955, and for the widescreen versions of some Disney films, before 1.85:1 became the norm.

name: Widescreen
description: The shape of HDTVs, and of nearly all television made since the 2000s. It fills a modern TV screen exactly.

name: Flat
description: The standard non-anamorphic ("flat") widescreen shape for theatrical films in the US and UK, introduced by Universal in 1953. Only slightly wider than a TV screen.
Close to the full frame of a digital cinema projector (256:135, for example 4096 × 2160), a little wider than a TV screen.

name: IMAX Digital
description: The shape of digital IMAX screens, introduced in 2008, and of the full frame of a digital cinema projector. A little taller than standard theatrical widescreen, and often used only for selected scenes of a film.

name: Univisium
description: First used for RKO's Superscope in the 1950s, then proposed by cinematographer Vittorio Storaro in 1998 as a single shape for both cinema and television. Now common in streaming series.

name: 70 mm
description: The shape of standard 70 mm film prints, introduced with Todd-AO in 1955 and used for many roadshow epics.

name: Ultrawide
description: The marketing name for ultra-wide TVs and monitors (really about 2.37:1), close to the shape of scope films.

name: CinemaScope
description: The anamorphic widescreen shape of CinemaScope and early Panavision films, standard until 1970. Often still used as a label for later films that are really 2.39:1.

name: Ultrawide
description: The true shape of "21:9" ultra-wide TVs and monitors (64:27), close to the shape of scope films.

name: Scope
description: The modern anamorphic widescreen standard since 1970, often rounded to 2.40:1. A TV shows it with black bars above and below.

name: Scope
description: A rounded way of writing 2.39:1, the modern anamorphic widescreen standard, and the shape widescreen films are given on Blu-ray (1920 × 800). A TV shows it with black bars above and below.

name: Early CinemaScope
description: The CinemaScope frame of 1954 to 1956 (and of CinemaScope 55), before an optical soundtrack on the film narrowed it to 2.35:1.

name: Cinerama
description: The 1950s process that used three 35 mm projectors side by side to fill a huge, deeply curved screen.

name: Original CinemaScope
description: The full width of the first CinemaScope films of 1953, before soundtracks were added to the film itself in 1954.

name: Ultra Panavision 70
description: One of the widest formats ever in regular use: anamorphic 70 mm (first called MGM Camera 65), used for about ten films from 1957 to 1966, such as Ben-Hur (1959), and revived for The Hateful Eight (2015).

name: Polyvision
description: Three ordinary 35 mm pictures projected side by side, first used for Abel Gance's Napoléon (1927).
